screens.title: Sequential Logic Foundations
screens.narratorSegment: Sequential logic gives digital systems memory. Rather than producing outputs from only the present inputs, sequential circuits combine inputs with stored state to create behavior over time. In this lesson you will see how flip-flops store a single bit, how groups of flip-flops form registers, how counters and shift registers use simple feedback and clocking to produce sequences, and why timing parameters like setup and hold time determine the maximum clock rate. For example, a D flip-flop captures a data value at a clock edge and then holds it until the next capture; that simple action is the foundation of registers and state machines on an FPGA. You will also learn practical contrasts: why designers generally prefer D flip-flops in LUT-based FPGAs instead of JK flip-flops, and how a T flip-flop toggles to divide frequency. Finally, we connect these elements to the timing equation that limits clock frequency. Understanding these ideas helps you reason about pipelines, counters, data serialization, and how to avoid metastability when signals violate timing constraints. As you move through the lesson, notice concrete examples and small design checks that show how to apply the timing equation and how to choose the right flip-flop style for a given hardware task.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to name and explain the behavior of the common flip-flop types, design synchronous counters, and use shift registers for serial-parallel conversion. You will also be able to identify registers in HDL descriptions and reason about timing constraints that determine the maximum safe clock frequency. For example, after studying flip-flop timing you'll compute the required minimum clock period from clock-to-Q delay, combinational propagation delay, and setup time. These skills matter because they let you build reliable state machines, pipelines, and serial interfaces on an FPGA without encountering metastability or timing violations. Each objective pairs a skill with a small verification milestone so you can test your understanding in simulation or on hardware. As you progress, look for how each flip-flop behavior maps to register and counter designs, and practice the timing equation with concrete numbers to gain confidence.

screens.title: Sequential vs Combinational Logic
screens.narratorSegment: Start by contrasting combinational and sequential logic. Combinational logic computes outputs strictly from the present inputs; it has no memory and no concept of time beyond propagation delays. Sequential logic, by contrast, computes outputs from inputs plus stored state. That stored state is held in flip-flops and updated on clock events, which gives sequential circuits the ability to count, remember configuration bits, and implement state machines. A simple example is a two-cycle protocol: combinational logic alone cannot represent that a command arrived in the previous cycle, but a flip-flop can store that fact and influence future outputs. A common misconception is to treat registers as passive wires; they are active state elements that change only at clock edges. Another important point is that flip-flops isolate combinational stages: the output of one register becomes input to combinational logic, then to the next register, forming pipeline stages. This pipelining reduces the combinational delay per stage and increases maximum clock frequency when designed correctly. As a takeaway, ask yourself: when designing a datapath, which signals need to be remembered across cycles and which can be purely combinational? That decision controls your state element count and timing constraints.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Sequential = logic + memory + clocking; this enables behaviors that unfold over time.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Sequential vs Combinational Logic
Definition
Sequential logic uses stored state in addition to inputs to determine outputs. Memory elements update on a clock edge.
Example: A single flip-flop remembers whether an event occurred last cycle so the circuit can react differently this cycle.
Misconception: Registers are not wires. They only change value at clock edges, so timing rather than connectivity controls behavior.
Why it matters: State allows counters, pipelined datapaths, and finite state machines needed for protocols and control logic.
Key Takeaway

Decide which signals require memory; converting combinational logic into sequential stages changes timing and resource use.

Illustration: pipeline stage cards
Register
Stores a value on a clock edge. Output drives combinational logic until next clock.
Combinational Logic
Performs operations on values from registers; its propagation delay affects clock period.
Concrete scenario: a multiply-accumulate datapath split across two pipeline stages uses registers to hold intermediate results. This reduces logic depth per cycle, letting the design run at a higher clock frequency while preserving correctness—if timing for each stage meets setup and hold constraints.
Question: Which signals need to survive across cycles for your algorithm?
Practice: Mark registers in a block diagram and compute combinational delay per stage.

screens.title: D Flip-Flop: Behavior and Role
screens.narratorSegment: A D flip-flop captures the value present at its data input exactly on the active clock edge and then holds that value until the next active edge. This edge-triggered capture property means changes at the D input between clock edges are ignored; only the value around the clock transition matters. In FPGAs the D flip-flop is the standard building block: registers, counters, and state machines are all synthesized to arrays of D flip-flops. Practically, a register is just many D flip-flops sharing the same clock so you can store a multi-bit word. A useful mental model is that a D flip-flop implements one-bit memory with synchronous updates. An important misconception to avoid is thinking that D updates continuously; it does not. Also note common control signals found in FPGA flip-flops: clock enable lets you gate writes without affecting the global clock, synchronous reset clears the stored value at the clock edge, and asynchronous reset or preset forces the output instantly independent of the clock. These signals change how and when data is stored, so consider them when mapping HDL to hardware. For practice, imagine a pipeline register with clock enable used to freeze the pipeline when a stall is needed. How would that affect the data flow? That thought experiment clarifies the flip-flop's role in real systems.

keyIdea.title: D flip-flop
keyIdea.text: Edge-triggered capture of D on clock edge; forms the basis of registers and pipeline stages in FPGAs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › D Flip-Flop
Behavior
Captures D at the active clock edge and holds it until the next capture. Changes between edges are ignored.
Concrete example: A single-bit write-enable register stores a status flag at each rising clock edge when clock enable is asserted.
FPGA controls: clock enable, synchronous reset, asynchronous reset, and preset affect when and how the stored bit changes.
Misconception: The D input is not sampled continuously; only the value around the edge is relevant.
Key Takeaway

D flip-flops are the standard memory primitive; design decisions like enabling and resets determine write behavior in hardware.

Example: Register as 8 D flip-flops
An 8-bit register is eight D flip-flops that share a clock. On a rising edge, each D is captured and the 8-bit value becomes stable on outputs until the next edge.
Scenario: pipeline freeze
Use clock enable to prevent capturing new data, which effectively stalls the pipeline without gating the global clock and avoiding timing hazards.
Check your understanding
If you need to synchronously clear a register at the next edge, use synchronous reset; asynchronous resets change the value immediately and can violate synchronous assumptions if used carelessly.

screens.title: T and JK Flip-Flops
screens.narratorSegment: The T flip-flop toggles its output on each active clock edge when its T input is HIGH, and holds the output when T is LOW. Because toggling flips the stored bit, connecting T to constant HIGH produces a divide-by-two frequency divider — a handy building block for ripple counters or simple frequency division. A JK flip-flop generalizes set, reset, and toggle behavior with two inputs: J and K. When J and K are both zero the output holds; J=1 K=0 sets; J=0 K=1 resets; and J=K=1 toggles. Historically JK flip-flops were called universal because they can implement many behaviors, but in modern FPGA practice designers usually prefer D flip-flops because FPGA LUT architectures map D registers more directly and efficiently. A common student mistake is to try to synthesize JK flip-flops directly; synthesis tools will translate them to D-equivalents, which can hide extra logic cost. As a practical exercise, consider building a binary counter: using T flip-flops chained yields toggling behavior per bit, while implementing the same counter with D flip-flops requires XOR or combinational logic to compute the next state. Compare resource usage and timing in simulation to understand trade-offs.

keyIdea.title: T vs JK
keyIdea.text: T toggles for frequency division; JK can toggle, set, or reset but is less common in LUT-FPGA designs than D flip-flops.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › T and JK Flip-Flops
T Flip-Flop
Toggles output when T=1; holds when T=0. Useful for dividing clock frequency by two when T is tied high.
Concrete: tying T=1 yields a flip every clock, producing a square wave at half the input clock rate.
Use: simple ripple or synchronous counters where toggling is required.
JK Flip-Flop
J and K inputs allow set, reset, hold, and toggle behavior. When both are high you get toggle; other combinations map to set or reset.
Concrete: configure J=K=1 to toggle for counting, or use J/K combinations to implement conditional set/reset logic.
Misconception: JK is not inherently cheaper in modern FPGAs. Synthesis usually targets D flip-flops, so JK logic often becomes additional combinational resources.
Pro Tip

Prefer D flip-flops in LUT-based FPGAs; express toggle or JK behavior with D plus combinational logic for predictable resource use.

Compare implementations
Try both designs for a 3-bit counter: implement one with chained T flip-flops and another with D flip-flops plus XORs. Observe resource use and maximum clock achievable after synthesis.

screens.title: Registers and Multi-bit Storage
screens.narratorSegment: A register is simply a set of D flip-flops that share a clock to store multi-bit values. For example, an 8-bit register contains eight D flip-flops that capture the eight data bits on the active clock edge. In FPGA design registers are used to hold operands between pipeline stages, maintain processor state, and build FIFOs and buffers. Important control signals include clock enable, which allows conditional writes without gating the global clock, and synchronous reset which clears the register at the next clock edge. A typical mistake is trying to gate the clock directly to freeze data; this can create complex clock domains and timing hazards. Instead, use synchronous clock enable so the register still meets timing and is predictable. When designing pipelines, choose register boundaries to balance combinational delay per stage so each stage meets timing requirements. Registers are also key to building shift registers: link several registers in series and feed bits from one Q to the next D each clock to achieve shifting. As a practical exercise, imagine implementing an 8-bit pipeline where registers separate combinational blocks; compute the expected maximum clock by measuring logic delay per stage and applying the timing equation.

keyIdea.title: Register
keyIdea.text: A group of D flip-flops sharing the same clock to store multi-bit values; use clock enable not clock gating.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Registers & Multi-bit Storage
Register Anatomy
Multiple D flip-flops sharing a clock store a multi-bit value and present stable outputs between clock edges.
Example: 8-bit register captures a byte of data on each rising edge when write-enable is active.
Control: use clock enable to freeze values for stalls; avoid gating the clock signal directly.
Use case: pipeline boundaries, operand storage, and interim buffering in datapaths.
Concrete scenario
Split a complex combinational operation into two stages and insert registers between them. This halves combinational depth per clock, likely increasing achievable clock frequency if each stage meets timing.
Shift register building
Connect register outputs to the next register's inputs to create serial shifting of bits across clock cycles for SIPO or PISO implementations.
Common mistake
Gating clocks to disable writes can cause timing skew and clock domain issues; prefer synchronous enables to retain timing closure.

screens.title: Counters: Binary and Modulo-N
screens.narratorSegment: A counter is a sequential circuit that changes its stored value on each clock edge according to a counting rule. The simplest is a binary counter that increments every clock: 0000, 0001, 0010, and so on. Counters can decrement or follow other sequences. A modulo-N counter counts from 0 to N-1 and then wraps back to 0. Design typically uses flip-flops for storage plus combinational logic to compute the next state. One approach uses XOR gates and carry logic to generate the increment result when using D flip-flops. Another classic method chains T flip-flops so each stage toggles when less significant bits roll over. In FPGAs you generally describe counters in HDL and let the synthesizer map them to D flip-flops and LUTs. A practical example: design a 4-bit modulo-10 counter by adding combinational logic that resets the counter to zero when the binary count reaches 10. A common misconception is that ripple counters are always synchronous; ripple counters propagate toggles through flip-flops and create timing skew between bits. Use synchronous counters for precise timing and simultaneous updates. For a learning task, implement a 4-bit synchronous binary counter in HDL, simulate its waveform, and then modify it into a modulo-10 counter to see the wrap behavior.

keyIdea.title: Counters
keyIdea.text: Counters sequence stored values each clock; modulo-N counters wrap and require combinational detection logic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Counters: Binary and Modulo-N
Counting Process
Each clock edge updates the stored value according to increment/decrement logic implemented in combinational logic feeding D inputs.
Step 1: Flip-flops hold current count.
Step 2: Combinational logic computes next value (e.g., add 1).
Step 3: On clock edge D captures the next value and becomes the new count.
Key Takeaway

Synchronous counters update all bits at once; modulo counters need detection and reset or conditional next-state logic.

Concrete example: 4-bit modulo-10 counter
Detect binary 1010 and force next state to 0000. Implement this detection combinationally and feed the D inputs so the counter wraps on the next clock.
Misconception
Ripple counters are asynchronous between bits and can cause transient incorrect values during toggling; synchronous counters avoid this by computing the full next state for all bits simultaneously.
Try this
Implement both T-based and D-based counters for the same width and compare synthesized resource usage and timing margins.

screens.title: Shift Registers: SIPO and PISO
screens.narratorSegment: Shift registers move bits across a chain of flip-flops on each clock edge. In a serial-in, parallel-out shift register you input one bit per clock and read the entire register in parallel after N clocks, which is useful for serial receivers that collect bits into a byte. Conversely, a parallel-in, serial-out register loads an entire word in parallel and then shifts bits out one at a time for transmission. These structures are common in UART and SPI transmitters and receivers, and serve as simple delay lines or pattern generators. A useful concrete example is an 8-bit SIPO used in a UART receiver: eight serial bits arrive, each captured on the clock, and then the parallel outputs present the received byte for further processing. A frequent misconception is treating shift registers as combinational multiplexers; they are sequential and rely on clocked movement. Also remember that shift direction matters: left or right shifting changes the bit order and how feedback yields special counters like twisted-ring (Johnson) counters. Practice by designing a PISO that loads a byte and shifts it out, then verify timing and bit order in simulation.

keyIdea.title: Shift registers
keyIdea.text: SIPO loads serial data into parallel outputs; PISO loads parallel data and shifts it out serially, both using chains of flip-flops clocked each cycle.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Shift Registers: SIPO & PISO
Patterns
SIPO: serial input, parallel output. PISO: parallel input, serial output. Both implement shifting by wiring Q to the next D in series.
Use case: UART receiver uses SIPO to collect bits into a byte.
Use case: SPI master uses PISO to send a register's bits serially over MOSI.
Variation: Johnson counter feeds inverted last bit back to first to create 2N states and simple decoding.
Concrete example
Implement an 8-bit SIPO: on each clock capture the incoming serial bit into the least-significant stage and shift older bits up. After eight clocks, the parallel outputs present the full byte.
Misconception
Shifting is not instantaneous across stages; each clock moves bits one position and timing must ensure data is stable at capture windows.
Try this
Design a PISO to load a byte and shift it out, then simulate to verify bit order and clock alignment for the receiving device.
Real-world connection: shift registers map directly to serial interfaces on embedded boards and are simple to test with LEDs or logic analyzers.

screens.title: Timing Parameters: tsu, th, and tco
screens.narratorSegment: Timing parameters determine whether sequential logic captures the intended values. Setup time is the minimum interval before the clock edge that the D input must be stable; if the input changes too close to the edge, the flip-flop may sample an undefined value. Hold time is the minimum interval after the clock edge that D must remain stable; violating hold can also corrupt the captured value. Clock-to-Q delay is the time from the clock edge until the Q output becomes stable and available to downstream combinational logic. A practical contrast: setup time affects how early inputs must be prepared before capture, while hold time constrains how long sources must not change after the edge. keyIdea.text: Setup, hold, and clock-to-Q define safe timing windows; use them in the timing equation to avoid capture errors.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Timing Parameters
Key Definitions
Setup time (tsu): D must be stable for this minimum before the clock edge.
Hold time (th): D must remain stable for this minimum after the clock edge.
Clock-to-Q (tco): Delay until Q is valid after the clock edge.
Interpretation
Together these define when inputs must be stable and when outputs become usable. Violations lead to metastability or incorrect captures.
Worked calculation
Given tco, tpd, and tsu, compute minimum T_clock: T_clock > tco + tpd + tsu. For instance, if tco=3 ns, tpd=8 ns, tsu=2 ns, then T_clock > 13 ns so f_max ≈ 76.9 MHz. Running faster risks violating setup and producing metastability.
Misconception
Only looking at combinational delay ignores tco, which can make downstream registers sample invalid data if tco is long.
Try this
Compute the clock limit for several paths in your design. If a path is too slow, add registers to split combinational delay and recompute.
Real measurement: tools and timing reports provide tco and tpd estimates post-synthesis to guide clock choices and register placement.

screens.title: Timing Equation and Metastability
screens.narratorSegment: The timing equation T_clock > tco + tpd + tsu is the cornerstone of synchronous design. It states that the clock period must be longer than the sum of the clock-to-Q delay, the propagation delay of the combinational logic between registers, and the setup time of the receiving flip-flop. If you satisfy this inequality for all register-to-register paths, the design should capture correct values each cycle. When the inequality is violated, the receiving flip-flop may sample an input that is still changing, causing metastability — a state where the output takes an indeterminate time to resolve to a valid 0 or 1. In practice metastability is rare but damaging; it can propagate incorrect values and break protocols. A common example calculation from this chapter uses tco = 3 ns, tpd = 8 ns, tsu = 2 ns, giving T_clock > 13 ns or f_max ≈ 76.9 MHz. If you run at 100 MHz, the setup window is violated and the flip-flop may capture an incorrect value or become metastable. Mitigations include increasing the clock period, reducing combinational delay, or inserting pipeline registers. For interactive practice, compute path delays in your design, apply the equation, and plan where to place additional registers to meet timing requirements.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Timing Equation & Metastability
Equation
T_clock must be greater than tco + tpd + tsu for correct sampling across register boundaries.
Worked numbers: tco=3 ns, tpd=8 ns, tsu=2 ns → T_clock > 13 ns → f_max ≈ 76.9 MHz.
Consequence: running at 100 MHz violates setup and risks metastability or wrong captures.
Mitigations & Practice
Options: lengthen clock period, shorten combinational paths by adding registers, or restructure logic. In safety-critical paths, use synchronizers and allow extra settling time for asynchronous inputs to reduce metastability risk.
Practice
Identify the worst-case path in your design, compute tpd, include tco and tsu, and decide whether to pipeline or reduce logic depth.
Question
If a path violates timing by 2 ns, where would you insert a register to split the combinational delay and how does that change the equation?

screens.title: Johnson Counter: Hands-on Activity
screens.narratorSegment: The Johnson counter, or twisted-ring counter, is a practical hands-on project that combines shift registers and feedback. It uses an N-stage shift register where the complement of the last bit is fed back to the first stage. This arrangement produces 2N unique states for N flip-flops, which is often more states than a simple ring counter and yields simple patterns that are easy to decode. For example, a 4-bit Johnson counter produces eight distinct states. To design one, draw a shift register of N D flip-flops, route Q of bit N-1 through an inverter and feed it back into the first D. Write the Verilog by defining a register vector and on each clock assign its next value as {reg[N-2:0], not reg[N-1]}. Simulate to observe the state sequence and verify you get 2N states. Compare this to a standard binary counter: the Johnson counter often requires simpler decoding for certain sequences and can be useful for LED scanners or simple pattern generators. A common question is resource cost: it uses N flip-flops like a register but decoding logic differs. Implement, simulate, and then contrast state counts and decoding complexity to confirm why a Johnson counter is a compact alternative in some control tasks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Johnson Counter Activity
Design steps
Create an N-stage shift register, invert the last stage, and feed it into the first. Simulate to observe the 2N-state sequence.
Step: Draw state diagram showing transitions for each clock pulse.
Step: Write Verilog assigning next state as concat of internal bits and inverted last bit.
Step: Simulate and count distinct states to verify 2N behavior.
Concrete example: 4-bit Johnson
With N=4 you will see eight unique states. Decoding specific patterns can be simpler than decoding a binary counter for certain applications like LED sequences or detector windows.
Comparison
Johnson: 2N states, simple shift feedback. Binary: 2^N states, more complex decoding for some patterns. Choose based on state count and decoder complexity.
Try this
Implement both a 4-bit Johnson and a 4-bit binary counter; compare state counts and the logic required to detect a target state.
Assessment idea: show the Verilog simulation trace and ask which clock cycle corresponds to a given state value.

Always apply the timing equation across register-to-register paths to compute f_max, and if a path fails, add registers to split combinational delay or reduce logic depth. These checks will save debugging time on FPGA boards and produce reliable embedded designs. fullNarratorScript:
Sequential logic gives digital systems memory. Rather than producing outputs from only the present inputs, sequential circuits combine inputs with stored state to create behavior over time. In this lesson you will see how flip-flops store a single bit, how groups of flip-flops form registers, how counters and shift registers use simple feedback and clocking to produce sequences, and why timing parameters like setup and hold time determine the maximum clock rate. For example, a D flip-flop captures a data value at a clock edge and then holds it until the next capture; that simple action is the foundation of registers and state machines on an FPGA. You will also learn practical contrasts: why designers generally prefer D flip-flops in LUT-based FPGAs instead of JK flip-flops, and how a T flip-flop toggles to divide frequency. Finally, we connect these elements to the timing equation that limits clock frequency. Understanding these ideas helps you reason about pipelines, counters, data serialization, and how to avoid metastability when signals violate timing constraints. As you move through the lesson, notice concrete examples and small design checks that show how to apply the timing equation and how to choose the right flip-flop style for a given hardware task.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to name and explain the behavior of the common flip-flop types, design synchronous counters, and use shift registers for serial-parallel conversion. You will also be able to identify registers in HDL descriptions and reason about timing constraints that determine the maximum safe clock frequency. For example, after studying flip-flop timing you'll compute the required minimum clock period from clock-to-Q delay, combinational propagation delay, and setup time. These skills matter because they let you build reliable state machines, pipelines, and serial interfaces on an FPGA without encountering metastability or timing violations. Each objective pairs a skill with a small verification milestone so you can test your understanding in simulation or on hardware. As you progress, look for how each flip-flop behavior maps to register and counter designs, and practice the timing equation with concrete numbers to gain confidence.

These additional objectives focus on applying design patterns and verifying timing. You will learn to describe registers and counters in HDL so synthesis maps them to D flip-flops and LUTs, and you will practice creating modulo-N counters and examining how combinational logic delay affects clock period. You will also implement SIPO and PISO shift registers to convert between serial and parallel forms; this helps you design UART transmitters, SPI shift stages, or delay lines. Finally, you will measure or calculate setup, hold, and clock-to-Q delay values, and use them to set a maximum safe clock frequency. These are practical, testable abilities: write a small Verilog snippet for an 8-bit register, simulate a counter waveform, and run a timing calculation with sample numbers to confirm the clock constraint. Being comfortable with these tasks reduces design iterations and prevents common timing faults on FPGA boards.

Start by contrasting combinational and sequential logic. Combinational logic computes outputs strictly from the present inputs; it has no memory and no concept of time beyond propagation delays. Sequential logic, by contrast, computes outputs from inputs plus stored state. That stored state is held in flip-flops and updated on clock events, which gives sequential circuits the ability to count, remember configuration bits, and implement state machines. A simple example is a two-cycle protocol: combinational logic alone cannot represent that a command arrived in the previous cycle, but a flip-flop can store that fact and influence future outputs. A common misconception is to treat registers as passive wires; they are active state elements that change only at clock edges. Another important point is that flip-flops isolate combinational stages: the output of one register becomes input to combinational logic, then to the next register, forming pipeline stages. This pipelining reduces the combinational delay per stage and increases maximum clock frequency when designed correctly. As a takeaway, ask yourself: when designing a datapath, which signals need to be remembered across cycles and which can be purely combinational? That decision controls your state element count and timing constraints.

A D flip-flop captures the value present at its data input exactly on the active clock edge and then holds that value until the next active edge. This edge-triggered capture property means changes at the D input between clock edges are ignored; only the value around the clock transition matters. In FPGAs the D flip-flop is the standard building block: registers, counters, and state machines are all synthesized to arrays of D flip-flops. Practically, a register is just many D flip-flops sharing the same clock so you can store a multi-bit word. A useful mental model is that a D flip-flop implements one-bit memory with synchronous updates. An important misconception to avoid is thinking that D updates continuously; it does not. Also note common control signals found in FPGA flip-flops: clock enable lets you gate writes without affecting the global clock, synchronous reset clears the stored value at the clock edge, and asynchronous reset or preset forces the output instantly independent of the clock. These signals change how and when data is stored, so consider them when mapping HDL to hardware. For practice, imagine a pipeline register with clock enable used to freeze the pipeline when a stall is needed. How would that affect the data flow? That thought experiment clarifies the flip-flop's role in real systems.

The T flip-flop toggles its output on each active clock edge when its T input is HIGH, and holds the output when T is LOW. Because toggling flips the stored bit, connecting T to constant HIGH produces a divide-by-two frequency divider — a handy building block for ripple counters or simple frequency division. A JK flip-flop generalizes set, reset, and toggle behavior with two inputs: J and K. When J and K are both zero the output holds; J=1 K=0 sets; J=0 K=1 resets; and J=K=1 toggles. Historically JK flip-flops were called universal because they can implement many behaviors, but in modern FPGA practice designers usually prefer D flip-flops because FPGA LUT architectures map D registers more directly and efficiently. A common student mistake is to try to synthesize JK flip-flops directly; synthesis tools will translate them to D-equivalents, which can hide extra logic cost. As a practical exercise, consider building a binary counter: using T flip-flops chained yields toggling behavior per bit, while implementing the same counter with D flip-flops requires XOR or combinational logic to compute the next state. Compare resource usage and timing in simulation to understand trade-offs.

A register is simply a set of D flip-flops that share a clock to store multi-bit values. For example, an 8-bit register contains eight D flip-flops that capture the eight data bits on the active clock edge. In FPGA design registers are used to hold operands between pipeline stages, maintain processor state, and build FIFOs and buffers. Important control signals include clock enable, which allows conditional writes without gating the global clock, and synchronous reset which clears the register at the next clock edge. A typical mistake is trying to gate the clock directly to freeze data; this can create complex clock domains and timing hazards. Instead, use synchronous clock enable so the register still meets timing and is predictable. When designing pipelines, choose register boundaries to balance combinational delay per stage so each stage meets timing requirements. Registers are also key to building shift registers: link several registers in series and feed bits from one Q to the next D each clock to achieve shifting. As a practical exercise, imagine implementing an 8-bit pipeline where registers separate combinational blocks; compute the expected maximum clock by measuring logic delay per stage and applying the timing equation.

A counter is a sequential circuit that changes its stored value on each clock edge according to a counting rule. The simplest is a binary counter that increments every clock: 0000, 0001, 0010, and so on. Counters can decrement or follow other sequences. A modulo-N counter counts from 0 to N-1 and then wraps back to 0. Design typically uses flip-flops for storage plus combinational logic to compute the next state. One approach uses XOR gates and carry logic to generate the increment result when using D flip-flops. Another classic method chains T flip-flops so each stage toggles when less significant bits roll over. In FPGAs you generally describe counters in HDL and let the synthesizer map them to D flip-flops and LUTs. A practical example: design a 4-bit modulo-10 counter by adding combinational logic that resets the counter to zero when the binary count reaches 10. A common misconception is that ripple counters are always synchronous; ripple counters propagate toggles through flip-flops and create timing skew between bits. Use synchronous counters for precise timing and simultaneous updates. For a learning task, implement a 4-bit synchronous binary counter in HDL, simulate its waveform, and then modify it into a modulo-10 counter to see the wrap behavior.

Shift registers move bits across a chain of flip-flops on each clock edge. In a serial-in, parallel-out shift register you input one bit per clock and read the entire register in parallel after N clocks, which is useful for serial receivers that collect bits into a byte. Conversely, a parallel-in, serial-out register loads an entire word in parallel and then shifts bits out one at a time for transmission. These structures are common in UART and SPI transmitters and receivers, and serve as simple delay lines or pattern generators. A useful concrete example is an 8-bit SIPO used in a UART receiver: eight serial bits arrive, each captured on the clock, and then the parallel outputs present the received byte for further processing. A frequent misconception is treating shift registers as combinational multiplexers; they are sequential and rely on clocked movement. Also remember that shift direction matters: left or right shifting changes the bit order and how feedback yields special counters like twisted-ring (Johnson) counters.
